# Advanced `ggplot2`

## Spatial Data

Maps are more interesting than you think!

- The world isn't flat!

. . . 

This can get *intense*, but we will get by with simple features (`sf`)

## Map Projections

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UPaca-SrvEk width="80%" height="400px">}}

## WGS 84

[WGS 84](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Geodetic_System#WGS_84) is a 
robust and widely-used way of creating maps from 3D coordinates. 

- Good default
- Convert existing `sf` using `sf::st_transform(4326)`

. . . 

Not universal!

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L9Di-UVC-_4 width="40%" height="200px" >}}

NYC also has a bespoke projection optimized for local accuracy 

## sf Package

The `sf` package provides tools for dealing with spatial data: 

- `st_read` for reading `geojson` or `shp` files
- `st_join` for combining spatial data
- Integrates with `ggplot2::geom_sf()`  for plotting

## sf Objects

`sf` object - `data.frame` with additional _geometry_ information 

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(sf); library(tidyverse)
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package="sf"))
```

---

```{r}
#| echo: true
glimpse(nc)
```

This last row-`geometry`-is where the magic happens.

## Map Visualization

`sf` integrates well with `ggplot2`: 

- `geom_sf` knows how to handle geometries
- other features all work as expected (fill, animation, legends, *etc.*)

. . . 

::: {.small}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|2|3"
ggplot(nc, 
       aes(geometry=geometry)) + 
  geom_sf()
```

:::

## Chloropleths

A map whose fill depends on the value of interest is called a _chloropleth_:

::: {.small}

```{r}
ggplot(nc, aes(fill=BIR79 / BIR74 - 1, geometry=geometry)) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  guides(fill="none") + 
  ggtitle("% Change in Number of Children Born Per Year 1974-1979")
```

:::

From the Greek for 'color-abundance'  ("pleth" as in "plethora")

# Animation

## Animated Graphics

`gganimate` is the *de facto* standard for animated `ggplot2`: 

- Make a bunch of `png` files
- Combine into a `gif`

. . . 

Most commonly: `+transition_time(VARIABLE)`

**NB:** Unlike `facet_wrap`, no `~` before `VARIABLE`

## transition_*() functions

Animation is implemented via a new plot element: `transition_*()`: 

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
library(gganimate)
ggplot(births, aes(x=day_of_year, y=births)) +
  geom_line() + 
  transition_time(year)
```

## transition_*() functions

Add a title to indicate _time_ being shown: 

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
library(gganimate)
ggplot(births, aes(x=day_of_year, y=births)) +
  geom_line() + 
  transition_time(year) + ggtitle("Year: {frame_time}")
```


## transition_*() functions

`gganimate` "tweens" (interpolates) between frames for
smoothness - works best for _continuous_ time data. 

It's a bit weird here and we might prefer a more discrete
interpolation:

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
library(gganimate)
ggplot(births, aes(x=day_of_year, y=births)) +
  geom_line() + 
  transition_states(year) + ggtitle("Year: {closest_state}")
```

## Easing

Use the `ease_` functions (or `enter_()`/`exit_*()` separately) for finer control: 

```{r}
ggplot(births, aes(x=day_of_year, y=births, group=year)) +
  geom_line() + transition_states(year, transition_length = 4, state_length=1) + 
  ggtitle("Year: {closest_state}") + enter_grow() + exit_fade()
```

## Grouping

The `group`  variable is used to determine whether something is permanent over time. 

```{r}
penguins |> drop_na() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point() + ggtitle("{frame_time}") + 
  transition_time(year)
```

. . . 

**Bad!** Doesn't make sense to _interpolate_ penguins

## Grouping

```{r}
penguins |> drop_na() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_dep, y = body_mass, group=year)) +
  geom_point() + ggtitle("{floor(frame_time)}") + 
  transition_time(year)
```

See [`gganimate` Getting Started
Documentation](https://gganimate.com/articles/gganimate.html) 
for more

## Animated Graphics

When it works, `gganimate` is great

- PITA when external software is busted

. . . 

Alternatives:

# Interactivity

## Interactivity 

The `ggiraph` package provides for _interactive_ `ggplot2` 

- Principally focused on `tooltips` (mouseover) and simple click actions


Not _full dashboards_ - those come next

. . . 

Basic workflow: 

- Replace 'standard' `geom` with interactive alternatives (`geom_point()` to `geom_point_interactive()`)
- Add `tooltip` or `data_id` `aes`thetics
- run through `ggiraph::giraph()` before rendering


## ggiraph

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|3|4|5"
library(tidyverse); library(ggiraph)
g <- ggplot(penguins, 
       aes(x=flipper_len, y=body_mass, color=species, tooltip=species)) + 
  geom_point_interactive()
girafe(g)
```

Here `tooltip` specifies mouseover message

--- 

Use standard `ggplot2` customization and extensions: 

```{r}
#| echo: true
g <- g + theme_bw() + scale_color_brewer(name="Species", palette=2, type="qual") + 
         xlab("Flipper Length (mm)") + ylab("Body Mass (g)") + theme(legend.position="bottom")
girafe(g)
```

---

To 'correlate' elements, use `data_id`: 

```{r}
g <- ggplot(penguins, 
       aes(x=flipper_len, y=body_mass, 
           color=species, tooltip=species, data_id=species)) + 
  geom_point_interactive()
girafe(g)
```

---

Can even link across facets:

```{r}
girafe(g + facet_wrap(~island))
```


--- 

Or even more complex panels (in conjunction with `patchwork`)

::: {.smaller}
```{r}
library(patchwork) # Lets us 'add' plots together
g_basic <- ggplot(penguins, aes(color=species, tooltip=species, data_id=species))
g1 <- g_basic + geom_point_interactive(aes(x=body_mass, y=flipper_len))
g2 <- g_basic + geom_point_interactive(aes(x=bill_dep, y=bill_len))
girafe(g1 + g2)
```
:::

--- 

With a bit of custom Javascript (beyond this class), can have custom `click` events: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(ggiraph)
library(dplyr)
library(glue)

g <- penguins |> 
    filter(!is.na(body_mass), 
           !is.na(bill_len), 
           !is.na(sex)) |>
    mutate(
        click_action = glue('window.open("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/{species}_penguin");'), 
        tooltip=glue("This is a {species} penguin from {island} Island! It weighs {body_mass} g and has a flipper length of {flipper_len} millimeters.")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=bill_len, y=body_mass, color=species)) +
      geom_point_interactive(
        aes(tooltip = tooltip,
            onclick = click_action),
        size = 2.5,
        alpha = 0.8) + 
    theme_bw() +
    labs(subtitle = "Hover for tooltip, Click any point to learn more",
        x = "Bill Length (mm)",
        y = "Body Mass (g)")
girafe(g)
```

## Alternatives

The `plotly` package provides a `ggplotly()` function which 
works similarly. 

. . . 

Advantages: 

- Has a more sophisticated "time change" interactivity

. . . 

Disadvantages

- Doesn't support all of `ggplot2`
- `ggiraph` works well with (essentially) all `ggplot2` features


## Alternatives

`ggplotly` - `frame` gives rise to a time slider:

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2|4"
library(plotly)
G <- ggplot(births, aes(x=day_of_year, y=births, frame=year)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
ggplotly(G)
```

# Shiny

## Shiny

The `shiny` framework provides for *reactive* programming

- The system 'waits' for user input and responds accordingly, updating 
  (Think `Excel`)

---


```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| echo: false
#| viewerHeight: 420
library(shiny)
library(shinylive)
library(ggplot2)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive T-Test Power Calculator"),
  
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      numericInput("delta", "True Difference in Means (delta):", value = 0.5, step = 0.1),
      numericInput("sd", "Standard Deviation (sd):", value = 1.0, min = 0.1, step = 0.1),
      numericInput("n", "Sample Size per Group (n):", value = 30, min = 2, step = 1),
      numericInput("sig.level", "Significance Level (alpha):", value = 0.05, min = 0.001, max = 0.2, step = 0.01),
      selectInput("alternative", "Alternative Hypothesis:", 
                  choices = c("Two-Sided" = "two.sided", "One-Sided" = "one.sided")),
      selectInput("type", "Test Type:", 
                  choices = c("Two-Sample" = "two.sample", "One-Sample" = "one.sample", "Paired" = "paired"))
    ),
    
    mainPanel(
      h4(textOutput("powerText")),
      hr(),
      plotOutput("powerPlot")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  
  power_res <- reactive({
    power.t.test(
      n = input$n,
      delta = input$delta,
      sd = input$sd,
      sig.level = input$sig.level,
      alternative = input$alternative,
      type = input$type
    )
  })
  
  output$powerText <- renderText({
    res <- power_res()
    paste0("Estimated Statistical Power (1 - \u03b2): ", round(res$power * 100, 2), "%")
  })
  
  output$powerPlot <- renderPlot({
    max_n <- max(100, input$n * 2)
    n_seq <- seq(max(2, input$n %/% 2), max_n, by = 1)
    
    power_vals <- sapply(n_seq, function(n_val) {
      power.t.test(
        n = n_val,
        delta = input$delta,
        sd = input$sd,
        sig.level = input$sig.level,
        alternative = input$alternative,
        type = input$type
      )$power
    })
    
    df <- data.frame(n = n_seq, power = power_vals)
    current_power <- power_res()$power
    
    ggplot(df, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
      geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
      geom_point(aes(x = input$n, y = current_power), 
                 color = "firebrick", 
                 size = 4) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, 
                 linetype = "dashed", 
                 color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.8) +
      annotate("text", x = max(n_seq) * 0.75, y = 0.82, 
               label = "Target Power (80%)", color = "gray40",
               fontface = "italic") +
      labs(
        title = "Power Curve across Sample Sizes",
        subtitle = "Red dot highlights your current sample size selection",
        x = "Sample Size per Group (n)",
        y = "Statistical Power (1 - \u03b2)"
      ) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
      ylim(0, 1)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

---

New Concepts: 

::: {.incremental}

- `ui`: "front-end" specifies user-facing behavior
- `server`: "back-end" performs calculations in response to `ui` input
- `*Input` elements: takes user input and binds to a _reactive_ `R` variable
- `reactive` blocks: code that should be re-run in response to `ui` changes

:::

## Example - UI {.scrollable}

```{r}
      numericInput("sd", "Standard Deviation (sd):", value = 1.0, min = 0.1, step = 0.1),
      numericInput("n", "Sample Size per Group (n):", value = 30, min = 2, step = 1),
      numericInput("sig.level", "Significance Level (alpha):", value = 0.05, min = 0.001, max = 0.2, step = 0.01),
      selectInput("alternative", "Alternative Hypothesis:", 
                  choices = c("Two-Sided" = "two.sided", "One-Sided" = "one.sided")),
      selectInput("type", "Test Type:", 
                  choices = c("Two-Sample" = "two.sample", "One-Sample" = "one.sample", "Paired" = "paired"))
    ),
    
    mainPanel(
      h4(textOutput("powerText")),
      hr(),
      plotOutput("powerPlot")
    )

)
```

```{r}
  output$powerPlot <- renderPlot({

    n_seq <- seq(max(2, input$n %/% 2), max_n, by = 1)
    
    power_vals <- sapply(n_seq, function(n_val) {

    ggplot(df, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
```

# Plotting FAQs

## ggplot2 & Pie Charts

Why do Pie Charts have a bad reputation?

- Use of _area_ and _angle_ over _length_: less accurate perception
- Depends on `fill` to convey category - limited categories

. . . 

But primarily - "insider smugness"  and hate of `Excel`


## ggplot2 Plot Type Choice

For me: 

- Exploratory mode: 
  - Simple: line, scatter, bar, frequency
- Publication mode:
  - Very context specific
  - "Simplicity" / "Elegance" depend on audience expectations

## ggplot2 Font Sizing

Theme machinery!

```{r}
ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width)) + 
    geom_point() + theme(axis.text = element_text(size=24))
```

## Overplotting / ScatterBlobs

Student asked about "scatterblobs" - typo(?) but I love it!

. . . 

- Density based plotting: hexbins, histograms, rugplots
- Data reduction: summarization or sub-sampling

## Optimizing ggplot2 Performance

Active project of `ggplot2` team - not much you can do

. . . 

*Practical advice*: 

- Plot less (see previous slide)
- Take advantage of [`quarto` Caching](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/caching.html)

## ggplot2 Beyond Scatter and Line

Some favorite semi-advanced plot types: 

- Violin plots: combination of boxplot and histogram
- Ridgelines
- Beeswarms

_Deep_ rabbit hole

## ggplot2 + High-Dimensional Data

High-dimensional data: measure many variables per observation ("wide")

High-dimensional data is _hard_ to visualize

. . . 

Approaches: 

- Pair plots for "moderate" HDD
- PCA (or similar dimension reduction. Take 9890!)

## Custom ggplot2 Theme

```{r}
my_theme <- theme_bw() + theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = 'lightblue'))
ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) + geom_point() + my_theme
```

Advanced: 

- `theme_set()` - change `ggplot2` defaults for that session
- `.Rprofile` - set code to run every time you start `R`

## ggplot2 - When Not to Use 

`ggplot2` is designed to make good statistical graphics. Sub-par for: 

- Very advanced interactivity (unless combined with `shiny` or custom JS)
- _Really_ big data
- Hardcore customization / "infographics"
